title: Sell Mineral Rights in Greene County, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Greene County, PA
metaDescription: Greene County sits in the richest part of PA's Marcellus wet-gas fairway. We buy mineral and royalty interests around Waynesburg — honest numbers, no pressure.
heroLead: Greene County has some of the best Marcellus rock in the state, and mineral owners here know it — which is exactly why so many of them are frustrated with what actually lands in the mailbox.
intro: Greene County is where the Marcellus wet-gas window runs deepest and richest in Pennsylvania, and EQT has drilled it hard for well over a decade. Families around Waynesburg, Greensboro, and the smaller townships toward the West Virginia line often have a wall of royalty statements going back years — and just as often, a growing list of questions about why the number on line one keeps shrinking by the time it reaches the net-paid column.

We buy mineral and royalty interests throughout Greene County, whether you're holding producing acreage under an active EQT unit, a fractional interest split among heirs from a family farm, or ground that's leased but not yet drilled. If the coal-mining history of this county is also tangled up in your deed, we've seen that plenty of times too and know what to look for.

sections.heading: The deepest, richest corner of the Marcellus fairway
paragraphs: Greene County sits at the heart of the wet-gas Marcellus core, where the shale is thick, deep, and liquids-rich compared to counties further north. That's part of why operators have run some of the longest laterals and highest-producing units in the state through here, and why decline curves on Greene County wells tend to hold up better in the early years than in thinner, shallower parts of the play.

It also means spacing units in Greene County can pull in a lot of small tracts under one pooled unit, so it's common for a single family's acreage to represent a modest slice of a much bigger drilling unit rather than a standalone lease.

sections.heading: Coal country first, gas country second
paragraphs: Long before Marcellus, Greene County was — and still is — deep coal country, home to some of the largest underground longwall mines in the eastern United States. That history left its mark on title records the same way it did in Fayette County: coal, oil, and gas were frequently severed into separate ownership generations ago, and Waynesburg's Recorder of Deeds office holds decades of those old severance instruments.

If your family has farmed or held land here for multiple generations, there's a real chance the surface, the coal, and the oil and gas rights are no longer all in the same hands — worth confirming before you assume you know exactly what you're selling.

sections.heading: Why the royalty check never matches the lease percentage
paragraphs: The single most common call we get from Greene County owners is some version of the same question: the lease states an eighth, so why does the check come in smaller than that. The answer is almost always post-production deductions — gathering, compression, dehydration, and marketing charges the operator nets out before paying royalty, depending on how the lease was written. Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets a statutory 1/8 floor on the gross royalty owed, but the Kilmer v. Elexco decision left the door open for deductions to still apply on top of that floor in a lot of lease language.

Act 13 impact fees are a different, unrelated stream of money that Greene County and its municipalities receive per well for roads, water systems, and emergency services — it doesn't flow to individual royalty owners, so it never shows up on a royalty statement no matter how much local infrastructure it funds.

sections.heading: What drives value on Greene County acreage
paragraphs: Because this is such an active part of the play, well performance history matters more here than almost anywhere else in the state — a tract under a strong-producing EQT unit prices very differently than acreage that's leased but sitting in a queue for future development. Remaining primary term, pooling and unitization language, and whether your interest is producing, non-producing-but-leased, or open all factor in.

We won't quote a number sight unseen. Send us what you have — a lease, a division order, a recent royalty statement, or even just the well name if you know it — and we'll tell you plainly what we can offer and why.

faqs.question: Why is Greene County considered such a strong part of the Marcellus play?
faqs.answer: It sits in the deepest, most liquids-rich part of the wet-gas fairway, which generally supports stronger well performance than thinner or shallower parts of the formation. That's a general characteristic of the play here, not a promise about what any specific well or tract will produce.

faqs.question: My family's Greene County land has old coal leases too — does that affect an oil and gas sale?
faqs.answer: It can affect the title work, since coal, oil, and gas were often severed separately in this county's deeds. It doesn't usually stop an oil and gas sale, but we do want to see the relevant documents so we understand exactly what interest is being conveyed.

faqs.question: Are Act 13 impact fees paid to mineral owners in Greene County?
faqs.answer: No. Impact fees are paid by operators per well to the state, then distributed to counties and municipalities for infrastructure and services. They're a public-fund mechanism, not a payment to individual royalty owners, so they won't appear on your check.

faqs.question: What's a pooled or unitized interest and why does my Greene County lease mention it?
faqs.answer: Pooling combines multiple owners' tracts into one drilling unit so a single horizontal well can be produced across all of them, with each owner paid their proportionate share. It's standard in this part of the Marcellus play given how large modern units have become, and it directly affects how your royalty interest is valued.

faqs.question: Do you buy both producing and non-producing mineral interests in Greene County?
faqs.answer: Yes, we look at producing royalty interests, leased-but-undrilled acreage, and in some cases unleased minerals. What we can offer depends on the specifics, but we're happy to review any of these.
